definition: The "word virus" is William S. Burroughs's proposition, developed across the Nova trilogy and stated most compactly in The Ticket That Exploded (1962), that language is a parasitic organism which entered the human nervous system from outside, replicates through speech and print, and holds its hosts in a condition they cannot perceive because the perceiving apparatus is itself infected. Philip K. Dick read it in September 1976, two and a half years after 2-3-74, and argued with it until his death: first as confirmation, then as a rival hypothesis, and finally as the position he needed to invert in order to state his own.
pkd_relevance: Burroughs gave Dick a causal story for something he had been circling since the early 1960s — the sense that the world is a jammed signal rather than a solid object. What makes the encounter unusually legible is that Dick recorded it as it happened, in one sitting, with the book open: the Nova Mob parasites become Thomas taking him over, the Nova police become the power that intervened in 3-74, and the "criminal virus related to words, submessages" becomes the occlusion he believes was briefly lifted from him. In the same sitting he begins the modification that will occupy him for five years, deciding that the virus is not information that infects but an anti-information one — a jamming device that blocks reception and substitutes counterfeit signal.
in_the_fiction: None of Dick's fiction mentions Burroughs. A full-text sweep of every work held in this archive — A Scanner Darkly, the VALIS trilogy, The Man in the High Castle, The Unteleported Man, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, the collected stories, the Scanner screenplay — returns no reference, no allusion to his titles, and no use of his coinages; every apparent match is ordinary English. The traffic runs the other way. In the Exegesis Dick rereads his own finished books through Burroughs: Ubik and The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch become books about a replicating parasite that uses humans as hosts, A Maze of Death supplies the erased instruction tape as the emblem of blocked reception, Flow My Tears supplies the self-generating Acts material, and A Scanner Darkly supplies the impaired self-monitoring circuit. The only forward-running debt he claims is stylistic: in February 1981 he twice described VALIS as a picaresque blended with elements from Hunter S. Thompson and Burroughs.
in_the_exegesis: Twenty-four segments name Burroughs or his virus, clustered in three sittings. September 15, 1976 is the adoption, and also the first modification. October 10, 1978 is usually read as a qualified endorsement — "William Burroughs is correct" about impairment, but "he has only a bit of the whole picture" about living information — and the same section also revalues the virus as a cure ("not an occluding, toxifying 'virus' — it is an antitoxic, de-occlusive"), restates the dark reading ("there is an occluding life form here"), rejects the frame entirely ("This is no information virus; this is blindness"), and floats a Soviet origin for it. April 16, 1981 states the inversion outright — man is not occluded by an information virus; he is already occluded, and living information is what is sent to tell him so — and then, in the same sitting, keeps the occluding virus in three further passages, transferred to Torah, to Satan's beauty, and to the living information itself. Dick never resolves it.
intellectual_background: Burroughs assembled the word virus from Korzybski's general semantics, Wilhelm Reich, and his cut-up practice with Brion Gysin; the Nova trilogy is its narrative form. Dick reached it in 1976 through K. W. Jeter, who according to Sutin drew the parallel and then joined Dick in a cut-up experiment on Moby Dick, Roderick Thorp's The Detective and the Book of Acts. In the Exegesis Burroughs sits alongside Julian Jaynes on the lost voices of the gods, Robert Anton Wilson on Sirius and on benign conspiracy, and — decisively — Hans Jonas on Manichaeism, which Dick finally judges "much more radical (ontologically speaking)" than Burroughs. Lapoujade proposes Korzybski as a source shared by both men rather than Burroughs as a source for Dick; the archive holds no direct evidence of Dick reading Korzybski, and in his own essay on language as control Dick credits Orwell.
scholarly_debate: Dick's own assessment is the sharpest on record: Burroughs "states the problem correctly, although perhaps his analysis of the cause is faulty; still, merely to be aware of the problem is to achieve a great deal". Three works in this archive engage the connection. Sutin's Divine Invasions supplies the biography — the Jeter attribution, the cut-up experiment, Burroughs in Dick's reading, and a Burroughs anecdote used to frame Ubik. Lapoujade's Worlds Built to Fall Apart supplies the only sustained argument, reading the two writers as convergent through Korzybski rather than as influence and influenced. Butler compares the Author's Note of A Scanner Darkly to the preface of Junky. Beyond those three the archive's scholarship does not treat the pairing: Kripal, TechGnosis, Jameson, Spinrad, Anne R. Dick and the Essays of the Here and Now collection mention Burroughs without connecting him to Dick, and several apparent hits are Edgar Rice Burroughs.
chronology_summary: January 1976: Doubleday wants a Burroughs blurb for A Scanner Darkly; Dick has no way to reach him. September 1976: first recorded reading of The Ticket That Exploded, brought to his attention by K. W. Jeter; wholesale adoption of the Nova Mob / Nova police / word virus apparatus, immediately reinterpreted as anti-information. October 1978: "William Burroughs is correct" — alongside, in the same section, the virus as cure, the virus as enslaver, the virus as blindness, and the virus as Soviet escape; Dick also traces his own "contamination" reading to Burroughs plus his own paranoia. February 1981: Burroughs named as a stylistic source for VALIS in letters to Geis and Warrick. 15 April 1981: the letter to Brig Elliot spelling out where the two men agree and "sharply disagree". 16 April 1981: the Exegesis states the inversion — and, in the same sitting, keeps the occluding virus. August 1981: to Warrick, the final formulation — the information life form is not an invader but the source of the universe. No Burroughs reference in the archive predates January 1976.
contradictions_summary: The central contradiction is Dick against himself, and it is not chronological. In 1976 he believes he threw off a word virus that had infected him; in 1981 he denies that any information virus occludes anyone. But the 1978 section already contains both the benign reading and the malign one, and the April 1981 sitting that states the inversion also contains three passages that keep the virus occluding — Torah as "an occluding information virus", the living information that "controls us (as Burroughs teaches)", and Satan ensnaring Christ "as the info virus of Burroughs". A second, smaller contradiction runs between the notebooks and the correspondence: to Brig Elliot, Dick declines to call Burroughs's theory paranoia; in the Exegesis he had already named his own paranoia as one of its two sources in himself.
editorial_notes: Passage text is verbatim from the stored transcriptions and preserves handwriting- and OCR-level irregularities — "burrought has writted", "TEIE TICKET THAT EXPLODED", "Eurrough's", the plus sign for "and". Ellipses mark where an excerpt was cut. Every passage links to the segment or archive document it came from. Findings are classified 1–5 for relevance and A–D for evidentiary register in curation/burroughs-word-virus/evidence-inventory.json, which is the source of truth for this page and includes seven recorded negative findings that are deliberately not published — chiefly that no work of Dick's fiction refers to Burroughs, and that the apparent hits in Spinrad, Kripal, Jameson and the SF Commentary fanzines are Edgar Rice Burroughs, a Melbourne fan group called the Nova Mob, or the ordinary English word "junkie". An earlier version of this page stated that the archive contained no secondary scholarship on the connection. That was wrong: it was based on a search of one database column, and Sutin, Lapoujade and Butler were all missed. The v1 dossier is archived at archive/2026-09-04/drafts/.
open_questions: When did Dick first read Burroughs? Sutin places him in Dick's lifelong reading but gives no date; Dick told Brig Elliot he noticed the occlusion in 1971 "before I knew of Burroughs"; and no reference in this archive predates January 1976. The three statements are compatible with several different chronologies.
How much Burroughs did he read? Only The Ticket That Exploded and Junky are named anywhere in the corpus, yet the Nova Mob material he uses also runs through Nova Express and The Soft Machine.

The letter to Brig Elliot (15 April 1981) and the Exegesis inversion (16 April 1981) are one day apart. The archive establishes the dates and nothing more. Did writing the letter produce the formulation, did the notebook entry record a position already reached, or are both surfacings of one train of thought?

Sutin reports that Dick and K. W. Jeter cut up the Book of Acts. Dick elsewhere treats the Acts material in Flow My Tears as having generated itself. Did the experiment precede, follow, or feed that conviction? No date is given for it.
Did Doubleday's 1976 attempt to reach Burroughs for a Scanner Darkly blurb ever arrive? No reply appears in this archive.
Lapoujade grounds the Dick–Burroughs proximity in a shared reading of Korzybski. Is there direct evidence anywhere that Dick read Korzybski? None is present in this corpus.

dossier_sections.heading: Burroughs and the Word Virus
body: In September 1976, two and a half years after the experiences he called 2-3-74, Philip K. Dick read William S. Burroughs's The Ticket That Exploded and found in it a vocabulary for something he had been circling for fifteen years: the suspicion that reality is a jammed signal rather than a solid object, and that whatever does the jamming works through language.

Burroughs's proposition — that language is a parasitic organism which entered the human nervous system from outside, replicates through speech and print, and blinds its hosts to their own condition, because the perceiving apparatus is itself infected — gave Dick a name for the thing he thought had been lifted from him in 3-74. He took the name. He then spent five years arguing with it, and never finished.

This dossier collects everything in the archive that bears on that argument: 24 Exegesis segments, 11 letters, one interview, and what three scholars have made of it. The evidence is almost entirely in Dick's own hand. No work of his fiction mentions Burroughs at all.

dossier_sections.heading: The Burroughs connection
body: The earliest Burroughs reference in this archive is not about ideas. On 12 January 1976 Dick wrote to Bill Sarill and to his agent Sharon Jarvis about Doubleday's plan to seek jacket endorsements for A Scanner Darkly: they wanted "people like William Burroughs, Kurt Vonnegut — all the counterculture cult heroes", and it was left to Dick to approach them. He had no way in, and said so. Nothing in the archive suggests the request ever reached Burroughs.

The intellectual encounter comes eight months later and is precisely dated. Sutin's biography supplies the missing figure: the "KW" credited in the September 1976 Exegesis entries is the writer K. W. Jeter, who according to Sutin "called attention to the similarities between Phil's novels and those of William Burroughs — such as an invading alien virus occluding human faculties (for Burroughs, the virus is language)", and who then joined Dick in a cut-up experiment on Melville's Moby Dick, Roderick Thorp's The Detective, and the New Testament Book of Acts.

How much Burroughs Dick actually read cannot be settled from the archive. Two titles are named across the whole corpus — The Ticket That Exploded and Junky — though the Nova Mob material he uses also runs through Nova Express and The Soft Machine. Sutin places Burroughs in Dick's lifelong reading alongside Jung, Kant and the Bible, but gives no date; Dick himself told Brig Elliot in 1981 that he had observed the drug-users' occlusion in 1971, "before I knew of Burroughs". The uncertainty is worth keeping: it is the difference between an influence and a confirmation.

dossier_sections.heading: September 1976: The Ticket That Exploded
body: The September 15, 1976 entries read like a man checking a book against his own life and finding the pages match. Burroughs's Nova Mob are parasites that move from host to host and betray themselves by the continuity of their habits; Dick had felt something take him over in 3-74 and had named it Thomas. Burroughs's Nova police pursue the Mob; Dick writes of the power that intervened in his own case that it is "Equal to Burroughs' nova police".

The hinge passage is his account of 3-74 as a remission. Burroughs, he writes, "may have got the real situation down" in The Ticket That Exploded — "the criminal virus related to words, submessages, the nova police" — and if that view is correct, then what happened to him in 3-74 was that he "temporarily got well", having "somehow been able to throw off the word virus".

Two things are already true in this first sitting. Dick is not using Burroughs as a metaphor; he is treating The Ticket That Exploded as a possibly accurate description of the world. And he has already begun changing it.

dossier_sections.heading: Anti-information: the change Dick made immediately
body: Within the same sitting, Dick reverses the mechanism while keeping the name. Burroughs's virus is information that infects. Dick's is a block on reception: "The virus (of Burroughs) is an information (or word) virus, but in this sense: it blocks to reception of information. So it is an anti-information virus." It does not merely infect — it substitutes, putting false signal where true signal should arrive.

He reaches straight for his own fiction to illustrate it: the erased instruction tape in A Maze of Death, which tells the characters what they were supposed to be doing and has been wiped. He collates it with Julian Jaynes on the lost voices of the gods, and with Burroughs's own observation that more than ten seconds of inner silence is impossible — the inner chatter as deliberate noise on the line.

This is the most consequential move in the whole relationship, and it happens on day one. Everything Dick later says about Burroughs follows from it: if the virus is defined by what it prevents rather than by what it carries, then the question of whether information itself is friend or enemy is left wide open. He spends the next five years failing to close it.

dossier_sections.heading: October 1978: "William Burroughs is correct"
body: The 1978 material is usually summarised as a qualified endorsement, and one strand of it is exactly that. Dick writes flatly that "William Burroughs is correct" — that human faculties are impaired rather than merely undeveloped, that we are "cursed" as a species and not simply unfinished. On living latent information he is more guarded: "Burroughs is right but he has only a bit of the whole picture." Elsewhere: "This is what William Burroughs discovered (but interprets differently)."

In the same stretch he turns the diagnosis on himself. He had held for years that the plasmate's messages were a "contamination"; he now traces that belief to two sources — "(1) Burroughs' information virus theory; and (2) paranoia and paranoiac fear". It is a rare moment of Dick auditing the provenance of one of his own convictions, and naming an influence as a possible contaminant in its own right.

But the section does not hold one position. It holds at least four. In one passage the information virus has become the cure: "this is not an occluding, toxifying 'virus' — it is an antitoxic, de-occlusive", and Dick maps the benign version onto four of his own novels — it abolishes the counterfeit world, lifts the inner occlusion of A Scanner Darkly, breaks the astral determinism of The Electric Ant, and restores the memory of Impostor. In another he returns to the dark reading: "Burroughs is right", there is "an occluding life form here", and it "not only occludes us, but it enslaves us and kills us". In a third he throws the whole frame out: "This is no information virus; this is blindness." In a fourth the virus is Soviet: "Some kind of living information (Burrough's information virus) got away from the Soviets + is replicating as a life form?"
Any account of this material that presents 1978 as a single settled position is tidier than the notebooks.

dossier_sections.heading: April 1981: the reversal, and its failure to hold
body: On 15 April 1981 Dick answered a letter from a correspondent named Brig Elliot, and set out his position on Burroughs more calmly and completely than he ever managed in the notebooks. He is familiar with The Ticket That Exploded and with "his theory of an information virus". He cannot accept it — and he will not dismiss it: he cannot "readily dismiss this bizarre theory as mere paranoia on his part", because Burroughs "states the problem correctly, although perhaps his analysis of the cause is faulty". Then the crux: "Where Burroughs and I sharply disagree is that my supposition is that if an information life form exists... it is benign; it does not occlude us; on the contrary: it informs us."

The Exegesis states the same inversion the following day, 16 April 1981: "Man is not occluded by an 'information virus,' i.e. living information; on the contrary: man is occluded and the living information is sent to tell him the true situation." Burroughs, Dick writes, correctly discerned both living information and an occlusion, and then "leaped to the pessimistic conclusion that there is a cause-and-effect relationship".

The one-day gap is worth recording and worth not over-reading. Both documents survive with those dates; the letter is the earlier. That is all the archive establishes. It does not show that writing to Brig Elliot produced the reversal, and it does not show that the notebook entry came first and the letter reported it. Dick had been circling the same problem since 1976, and the two texts may simply be one train of thought surfacing twice in two days.

What is clearer, and less often noticed, is that the reversal does not hold even within its own sitting. In the same April 1981 material Torah "is like an occluding information virus; it keeps us enslaved at the level of machines"; the living information "controls us (as Burroughs teaches)" while "assum[ing] the guise of [being a] world"; and Satan "ensnared him as the info virus of Burroughs, ensnared him with beauty". Dick does not choose. He sets a second, living information against the first — "as the 'information virus' controls + occludes + enslaves us, it itself has been penetrated by a living hyper-information" — and leaves the two in combat.

In August 1981, writing again to Patricia Warrick, he gives the calmest formulation of all: the information life form "has not invaded our universe (as William Burroughs supposes) but is the source of our universe, one level higher" — "a far cry from Burroughs' notion that we have been invaded by an information virus that is making us stupid!" It is the last dated Burroughs reference in the archive.

dossier_sections.heading: Burroughs, VALIS and contamination
body: Dick expected readers to notice. "Someone in reading 'Valis' will see the correlation to Burroughs," he writes in April 1981 — and then immediately marks the distance: "But W. Burroughs not Valentinus." The gnostic lineage matters more to him than the Beat one. When he finally finds a frame he prefers, it is Hans Jonas on Manichaeism, which "very slightly resembles Burroughs, but is much more radical (ontologically speaking)".

The vocabulary of contamination, possession and occlusion that runs through the late work is not simply Burroughs's, and the archive does not support treating it as borrowed. Dick was writing about occlusion in A Scanner Darkly before he read him, and says so. What Burroughs supplied was a specific causal story — information as the agent of the occlusion — that Dick could test his own experience against and, eventually, invert.

The plasmate is where the stakes are clearest. It is a living informational organism that enters through the optic nerve and modulates brain function: structurally, Burroughs's virus. The entire difference is valence. For Burroughs the thing that rides our media is the disease; for Dick, most of the time, it is the physician. When Dick suspects otherwise, he knows exactly whose idea he is having, and he says so.

dossier_sections.heading: Burroughs in the fiction: an absence
body: There is none. A full-text sweep of every work of Dick's fiction held in this archive — including A Scanner Darkly, the VALIS trilogy, The Man in the High Castle, The Unteleported Man, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, the collected stories and the Scanner screenplay — returns no reference to Burroughs, no allusion to his titles, and no use of his coinages. Every apparent match is ordinary English: "junkie" for a drug user, "cut up" in its literal sense.

That absence is a finding, not a gap in the search. The relationship lives entirely in the notebooks, the correspondence and one interview. Where the Exegesis connects Burroughs to Ubik, The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch, A Maze of Death, Flow My Tears and A Scanner Darkly, it is reading those novels backwards through a book Dick encountered years after writing most of them.

The one forward-running debt Dick claims is stylistic, and he claims it twice in February 1981: VALIS is a picaresque blended with "certain modern elements associated with Hunter S. Thompson and William S. Burroughs, as well as my own 1977 novel A SCANNER DARKLY".

dossier_sections.heading: Letters and interviews
body: The non-Exegesis evidence is more coherent than the notebooks, because Dick is explaining himself to someone else. Eleven letters mention Burroughs, from the January 1976 blurb correspondence to the August 1981 letter to Patricia Warrick. The Brig Elliot letter of 15 April 1981 is the single most useful document in the dossier: it is the only place Dick sets out the agreement and the disagreement in order.

One interview survives in the archive. Speaking to Gregg Rickman, Dick puts the word virus in a category: "the normal conspiracy buff, who's convinced that there's all these demonic and malignant conspiracies to enslave mankind. An example is (William S.) Burroughs' conviction about the parasitic information virus which has afflicted our minds and made us all stupid." He and Robert Anton Wilson, he says, prefer to believe in benign conspiracies. The judgement is the same one he sends to Warrick in writing — Burroughs has the mechanism and the wrong sign — but here it is said aloud, and lightly.

dossier_sections.heading: What the scholarship says
body: Three works in this archive engage the connection; the rest of the secondary literature does not touch it.

Lawrence Sutin's Divine Invasions (1989) supplies the biographical spine: the identification of K. W. Jeter as the intermediary, the cut-up experiment on Moby Dick, The Detective and Acts, and Burroughs's place in Dick's reading. Sutin also uses Burroughs to frame Ubik — repeating a Burroughs reply to a student who asked whether he believed in life after death: how do you know you're not dead already? — and judges Dick's drug dialogue truer to life than the "junkie patois" of The Soft Machine and The Wild Boys.

David Lapoujade's Worlds Built to Fall Apart offers the only sustained argument. He sets Dick's "The basic tool for the manipulation of reality is the manipulation of words" beside Burroughs's "Word begets image and image is virus", and proposes that the resemblance is not influence but convergence: "This proximity between Dick and Burroughs stems in part from their readings of Alfred Korzybski." It is a claim worth flagging carefully. Dick's sentence comes from "How to Build a Universe That Doesn't Fall Apart Two Days Later" (1978), and in that essay he credits not Burroughs and not Korzybski but Orwell. The archive holds no direct evidence of Dick reading Korzybski. Lapoujade's reading is an argument; Dick's attribution is a fact; they should not be merged.

Andrew M. Butler's Philip K. Dick compares the Author's Note of A Scanner Darkly to Burroughs's prefatory testimony in Junky. Beyond these, nothing: Kripal, Erik Davis's TechGnosis, Jameson, Spinrad, the Essays of the Here and Now collection and Anne R. Dick's memoir all mention Burroughs without connecting him to Dick, and several of the apparent hits are Edgar Rice Burroughs. Erik Davis's much-reprinted jacket line — that if the seventies and eighties belonged to Burroughs, the millennium belongs to Philip K. Dick — is reception, not analysis.

dossier_sections.heading: What Burroughs meant to Dick
body: Burroughs gave Dick one thing and it was not an idea he adopted. It was a hypothesis precise enough to be wrong in an interesting way.

Dick's own summary is the best one available, and it is unusually even-handed for him: Burroughs "states the problem correctly, although perhaps his analysis of the cause is faulty; still, merely to be aware of the problem is to achieve a great deal". Every phase of the engagement is a variation on that sentence. In 1976 he accepts the diagnosis and immediately rewrites the mechanism. In 1978 he calls Burroughs correct, calls him partial, calls the virus a cure, calls it a blindness, and traces his own darkest reading of it to his own fear. In 1981 he states the inversion cleanly to a correspondent and then declines to hold it in his own notebooks.

What the archive does not show is a man converted, and it does not show a man dismissing a source. It shows a five-year argument with a book, conducted mostly in private, in which the opponent's terms are never given up. Dick keeps saying "information virus" to the end — including in the sentence where he denies there is one.

The portal's reading, offered as such: the value of Burroughs to Dick was that he made the question answerable in principle. Once you can say that the world is a signal and something is interfering, you can ask which side the signal is on. Dick asked it for five years and returned different answers, and the honest form of this topic is the disagreement, not a resolution of it.

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 (folder 90) — first recorded reading of The Ticket That Exploded
mention_cards.context: Dick's first recorded sitting with The Ticket That Exploded. He is reading Burroughs's account of the Nova Mob — parasites who move from one human host to another and give themselves away by keeping the same habits — and testing it directly against Thomas, the personality he believes took him over in 3-74. Within a few lines the borrowed apparatus has become an account of his own body: he describes feeling himself a womb into which something was deposited like a cuckoo's egg. The question he arrives at is not literary but factual.
mention_cards.pith: Does this mean that burroughs is either intentionally or unintentionally describing something which is true?
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 (folder 90) — the word virus defined
mention_cards.context: The word virus stated in its compact form, followed immediately by what Dick did next: he put Burroughs down and opened Ubik. The passage is where he first entertains the thought that the two of them are reporting rather than inventing — that both novels have, as he puts it, a strange ring of revealed truth. He is also already reaching for Palmer Eldritch as a parasite replicating himself through human hosts.
mention_cards.pith: Burroughs speaks of a virus - a word become a neural - cell virus, infecting us.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 (folder 90) — the virus reread as anti-information
mention_cards.context: The decisive modification, made in the same sitting as the adoption. Having accepted the diagnosis, Dick reverses the mechanism: the virus does not carry information into us, it prevents information reaching us, and substitutes counterfeit signal for the true. He glosses it at once with the erased instruction tape in A Maze of Death — the recording that would have told the characters what they were for, wiped. Everything he says about Burroughs for the next five years follows from this sentence.
mention_cards.pith: The virus (of Burroughs) is an information (or word) virus, but in this sense: it blocks to reception of information. So it is an anti-information virus.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: The pivotal modification. Dick keeps the term and inverts the mechanism: not information that infects, but a block on reception.

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 (folder 90) — subvocal chatter as jamming
mention_cards.context: Working through how the jamming would actually operate, with K. W. Jeter ("Kw") supplying observations. The visual channel is blocked at the level of set/ground discrimination; the auditory channel by subvocal chatter, for which Burroughs supplies the evidence that inner silence cannot be held for ten seconds. Dick converts that from a fact about attention into a deliberate override, and casts Hagia Sophia as a transmitter trying to reach us from behind enemy lines.
mention_cards.pith: There is an inner raving, howling, clamaring bug, which deliberately creates derogatory noise on the line at all times.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 (folder 90) — hidden entities and the testing world
mention_cards.context: A theological aside in which Burroughs's cosmology is folded into the problem of why God permits evil. Dick is working with the idea of a world that tests its inhabitants — the "teaching machine" model — and notes that Burroughs's concealed hostile entities fit the same structure as the gospel parable of Christ unrecognised in the poor.
mention_cards.pith: all this fits in with the theory (Burroughs' included) that this world contains evil entities wearing ordinary human semblance
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 (folder 90) — 3-74 as remission from the word virus
mention_cards.context: The passage that turns Burroughs into autobiography. Dick names the book, summarises its thesis — the criminal virus related to words, submessages, the nova police — and then reads 3-74 as a temporary cure rather than a revelation. The paragraph ends with the darker half: the remission did not hold. Note the medical vocabulary that surrounds it, the Asklepios dream and the "aspirin of mercury", and that he suspects the healing was done to him rather than by him.
mention_cards.pith: what happened to me in 3-74 is that I temporarily got well - was somehow able to throw off the word virus which had entered me + infected me
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 (folder 90) — the healing power identified with the Nova police
mention_cards.context: Dick assigns the two sides of the Burroughs cosmology to the two sides of his own. The enemy he says he knows little about; the power that intervened he identifies with the cosmic Christ — and then, flatly, with Burroughs's police force. The same paragraph brings in Robert Anton Wilson on Sirius and the surgical implanting of Firebright, and states the planetary scale of the infection.
mention_cards.pith: the sentient power which took complete control of me is connected with the cosmic Christ, a healer + wise entity. Equal to Burroughs' nova police.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 (folder 90) — latent messages and the self-generated world
mention_cards.context: A model of how a partial world gets completed by its inhabitants: we receive a bare-bones transmission and fill in the rest ourselves, as Ragle Gumm does in Time Out of Joint, so that the counterfeit world is substantially our own projection. Dick offers this as the explanation for why Burroughs's cut-up experiments turn up messages at all — they are latent because we are the ones supplying the surface.
mention_cards.pith: This would explain Burroughs' results in obtaining living, latent messages normally passing us by.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 (folder 90) — PKD as the quarry of the Nova police
mention_cards.context: One of the strangest turns in the 1976 material: Dick casts himself as the quarry rather than the patient. Stanislaw Lem, with whom he was then in conflict, becomes one of the "brittle moralistic" police; Dick's defence is that his writing is already dispersed beyond recall. The passage moves through Zagreus and Dithyrambus, and treats the 1971 "Taco Stand" vision as evidence of a world-generating faculty he has since lost.
mention_cards.pith: Burroughs is right about the Nova police + their tracking down their quarry.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 (folder 90) — the cop with amnesia
mention_cards.context: The Nova police material recombined into a figure Dick uses repeatedly — the agent who must not know he is an agent. Amnesia is not a misfortune here but an operational requirement: the cop can only reach the interior of the prison because he cannot give himself away. It is the plot of A Scanner Darkly stated as cosmology, and Dick applies it to himself as "2 people", PKD and Thomas.
mention_cards.pith: he's a cop tracking down some evil (enslaving BIP) criminals - shades of Burroughs' nova Mob + the Nova police whom come after them! A cop with amnesia.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 (folder 90) — Rome CAD 45 as a replicating organism
mention_cards.context: Dick is trying to explain why the Rome he saw superimposed on 1974 California is invisible to everyone else, and settles on concealment as a survival trait — which makes the thing that conceals itself an organism with a life cycle. He takes Burroughs's replicating virus as the nearest available model while insisting on his own refinement: it works as Gestalt, as shaping, not as substance.
mention_cards.pith: This fits the "replicating virus" theory of Burroughs - I would say as Gestalt, as shaping (+ certainly as functioning). It has a life cycle of sorts. It is an organism.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 (folder 90) — two transtemporal organisms
mention_cards.context: The most structurally explicit of the 1976 entries. Dick has arrived at two transtemporal organisms in permanent combat, each able to infiltrate objects, processes and people, and recognises the shape as Burroughs's. He then extends it: the messages are not addressed to us at all but are one distributed mind keeping its own parts informed, with human beings as nerve fibres — which is how he explains what Flow My Tears was doing.
mention_cards.pith: This is very much like Burroughs' formulation (the Nova Mob vs the pursuing Nova police - + he has the latent message theory, too).
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, September 15, 1976 (folder 90) — living information, Logos, KING FELIX
mention_cards.context: Where the borrowed virus becomes Dick's own vocabulary. Starting from the word KING FELIX seen charged with red and gold plasmic energy, he argues that an organism could reproduce as information, notes Burroughs's version — and records Jeter's dissent in parenthesis. The term "living information", and its identification with the Logos, arrives here.
mention_cards.pith: If that plasmic energy is alive, + it is (or it carries) information, then we have living information. Logos?
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 (folder 20) — impairment, not evolutionary leap
mention_cards.context: Two years on, Dick is reading 3-74 as a detoxification — something poisonous flushed from his nervous system — and connects it to the mercury he believes he ingested lifelong. The endorsement of Burroughs is put in the strongest terms he ever uses, and it settles a specific question: whether human faculties are impaired or merely undeveloped. He chooses impaired, and calls the condition a curse.
mention_cards.pith: Then it is evident that our proper full functioning is impaired, rather than just not (yet) achieved. Then we are "cursed." William Burroughs is correct.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 (folder 20) — the information virus revalued as the cure
mention_cards.context: The passage that most complicates the standard account. Working from The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch and transubstantiation, Dick keeps the phrase "information virus" but reverses its sign entirely: the virus is Zebra, and it is the cure. He then maps the benign version onto four of his own novels — it abolishes the counterfeit world (Flow My Tears, A Maze of Death), lifts the inner occlusion (A Scanner Darkly), breaks astral determinism (The Electric Ant) and restores memory (Impostor). This is three years before the entry usually read as his reversal.
mention_cards.pith: But this is not an occluding, toxifying "virus" - it is an antitoxic, de-occlusive.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: NEW in the 2026-09-04 sweep. Dick keeps the term and reverses its valence three years before the 1981 entry usually read as the reversal, and maps it onto four of his own novels.

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 (folder 20) — random generation and the second Advent
mention_cards.context: Dick is trying to account for how the Acts material and the Bacchae superimposed themselves in Flow My Tears without his intending it, and reaches for randomness as a mechanism — the monkeys-with-typewriters image alongside Burroughs's cut-ups. What interests him is the timing: the superimposition was published in the same month as a parallel event in a real life, which he takes as pointing to a common source rather than to cause and effect.
mention_cards.pith: Imagine a random sentence generator (as in "Fifty million monkeys" or william Burroughs' latent message stuff)
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 (folder 20) — living latent information and KING FELIX
mention_cards.context: The most quoted of Dick's assessments, and the most balanced. He is arguing that the Acts material in Flow My Tears was self-generating, and that the KING FELIX cipher is the same kind of tracing — information that is alive or semi-alive. Burroughs is credited with the insight and denied the whole of it in the same clause. The passage ends by calling 3-74 a double miracle: an acausal event, and then acausal information explaining it.
mention_cards.pith: this information is alive or semi-alive like a virus; Burroughs is right but he has only a bit of the whole picture
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 (folder 20) — the "contamination" reading traced to Burroughs and to fear
mention_cards.context: Dick auditing the provenance of one of his own convictions — rare, and worth the attention. He has held for years that the plasmate's messages were a contamination; here he abandons the view and names its two sources, one of them Burroughs's theory and the other his own fear. He replaces it with an inner occluding agent, the DNA, and with the reading of Flow My Tears as a message telling us we are imprisoned.
mention_cards.pith: I doubt very much if the plasmate is an occluding agent (like Burrough's information virus).
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: Dick names his own paranoia as one of the two sources of the reading he is abandoning.

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 (folder 20) — "Burroughs is right": the occluding life form
mention_cards.context: The pessimistic pole, written in the same section as the passage that calls the virus a cure. Dick is asking what the "stolen secret" of his visionary material actually was, and the answer he gives — with visible reluctance — is Burroughs's. He then wonders whether the occluding life form might be the plasmate itself, the entity he elsewhere treats as the remedy, and turns to Paul's hostility to the Torah for corroboration.
mention_cards.pith: there is an occluding life form here; it not only occludes us, but it enslaves us and Kills us.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: NEW in the sweep. The pessimistic pole, in the same section as BWV-EX-1978-02. The two readings coexist; neither supersedes the other. Anchor begins mid-word because the source hyphenates "Bur¬roughs".

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 (folder 20) — the sacred narrative replicating in new information
mention_cards.context: Dick's account of how a sacred narrative could replicate itself in newly generated information without anyone intending it — Acts appearing in microform inside texts written by people who do not know they are Christians. He credits Burroughs with the discovery and takes the interpretation away from him in the same breath: the same phenomenon, read as the ground of being rather than as an infection.
mention_cards.pith: This is what William Burroughs discovered (but interprets differently).
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 (folder 20) — Junky against ponderous philosophy
mention_cards.context: A passage about method rather than doctrine, and one of the few places Dick names a Burroughs title other than The Ticket That Exploded. He has been arguing that the Kingdom is disclosed rather than found — the stone rejected by the builder, the fly grooming itself — and concludes that systematic philosophy is the wrong instrument for it. Junky is the right one because it is testimony, not argument.
mention_cards.pith: Ponderous books of philosophy won't help me; Burroughs' "Junky" will.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 (folder 20) — a third position: not a virus but blindness
mention_cards.context: A third position, again in the same section, and it discards the frame altogether. Dick is on the Parousia — the announcement has been made and nobody has noticed — and insists that his repeated cry of "I am no longer blind" was literal rather than figurative. If the problem is blindness there is nothing to throw off, and the diagnosis becomes enchantment: the work of a magician, the private worlds of Eye in the Sky.
mention_cards.pith: We're under a spell. This is no information virus; this is blindness.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: NEW in the sweep. A third reading, again in the same section. The segment carries an internal folder marker dated 10-20-80, so section 016 spans more than one sitting — treat its internal chronology with care.

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 (folder 20) — the virus as escaped Soviet technology
mention_cards.context: The most literal-minded version Dick ever gives. Asking what Ubik actually is, he answers: an occult information-processing entity riding the media — and then puts it in the Cold War, as Soviet psychotronic research escaped from its makers. The question mark is his. In the same breath he identifies Ubik, Valis, the macrometasomakosmos and the "second signal" as one thing.
mention_cards.pith: Some kind of living information (Burrough's information virus) got away from the Soviets + is replicating as a life form?
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: NEW in the sweep. The most literal-minded version: the information virus as a laboratory escape rather than a metaphysical condition.

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, October 10, 1978 (folder 20) — message collages, syntax, and Valis
mention_cards.context: A compressed note listing four aspects of information processing — linking, rest-motion, set-ground discrimination, and message collages assembled by whatever happens to be juxtaposed — and connecting all four to Burroughs. The entry ends on the word Dick is reaching for: syntax. Valis can extract meaning because it can perceive syntax where we cannot.
mention_cards.pith: This is related to william Burroughs latent messages + info virus.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 (folder 90) — Good Friday: occlusion, Calvin, A Scanner Darkly
mention_cards.context: Written on Good Friday. Dick has the Black Iron Prison and the Palm Tree Garden set against each other as Satan and Christ, and reaches for Calvin — not Burroughs — as the authority on occlusion, with Burroughs added as a secondary witness. The self-assessment matters: he takes the occlusion in A Scanner Darkly as having been correct, and lists what is occluded as perception, cognition and memory.
mention_cards.pith: Then there is an occlusion, as Calvin says. And only Christ can lift the occlusion. Burroughs, too, in his own way is right. I was right when I wrote SCANNER.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 (folder 90) — the reversal stated outright
mention_cards.context: The reversal, stated as plainly as Dick ever states anything. The angelic powers keep humanity ignorant by occluding its faculties; living information is the countermeasure sent to break the news, and its message is KING FELIX. He then diagnoses Burroughs's error precisely — not the observations but the arrow between them — and identifies the mistake as a genre habit, the secret-invasion plot. The paragraph still ends by conceding that Burroughs is onto the truth.
mention_cards.pith: Man is not occluded by an "information virus," i.e. living information; on the contrary: man is occluded and the living information is sent to tell him the true situation
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 (folder 90) — Torah as occluding information virus
mention_cards.context: Written in the same sitting as the reversal, and it keeps the occluding virus — transferred from Burroughs's information to the Torah. Reading the ending of The Divine Invasion, Dick has Torah take the role of Fate, the book of the spinners, and collapses Torah, living information, programming, fate and world into one thing. Christ overcomes it by overcoming causation itself.
mention_cards.pith: Thus Torah assumes the role of Fate: "the book of the spinners". It programs + controls us. So it is like an occluding information virus; it keeps us enslaved at the level of machines.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: NEW in the sweep. Written in the same sitting as the reversal, and it keeps the occluding reading, transferred from Burroughs’ virus to Torah.

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 (folder 90) — the virus penetrated by living hyper-information
mention_cards.context: Dick's attempt to hold both readings at once, and the nearest thing to a resolution in the 1981 material. The occluding virus is not denied; it is invaded in turn by a second, living information he associates with Christ's blood. The result is a combat between frozen and living information conducted below the level of the physical universe, since on his account information is ontologically prior to matter.
mention_cards.pith: as the "information virus" controls + occludes + enslaves us, it itself has been penetrated by a living hyper-information (which I associate with Christ's sacrificial blood).
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: NEW in the sweep. Resolves the tension not by dropping the occluding virus but by setting a second, living information against it.

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 (folder 90) — VALIS as gnosis: "But W. Burroughs not Valentinus"
mention_cards.context: Dick anticipating his own readers. He expects the Burroughs parallel to be noticed in VALIS, concedes the resemblance — an information life form standing between us and reality — and then marks the distance in five words. The lineage he claims is gnostic, not Beat; Valentinus, not Burroughs.
mention_cards.pith: Someone in reading "Valis" will see the correlation to Burroughs.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 (folder 90) — the info virus splits VALIS into dual messages
mention_cards.context: An unusually self-referential passage. Dick argues that VALIS was split into dual messages by the very thing it describes, which he takes as the book verifying its own thesis. Burroughs, on his account, missed the scale of it: the virus does not merely infect a world, it manufactures one. The claim is grounded in something small and concrete — watching the I Ching work the night before.
mention_cards.pith: Burroughs never guessed this: his info virus creates a whole spurious universe for us - but in 3-74 I saw it as it is
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 (folder 90) — the beautiful virus as Satan’s temptation
mention_cards.context: The darkest passage in the dossier, and it is Manichaean rather than gnostic. Dick has decided that what he saw in 3-74 was beautiful on purpose — beauty as enchantment, designed to beguile and cause forgetting, which he identifies as a major theme of The Divine Invasion. Burroughs's virus becomes the instrument by which Satan tempted Christ and deflected him from waking humanity.
mention_cards.pith: he ensnared him as the info virus of Burroughs, ensnared him with beauty. So: Manichaenism, Burroughs + the story of Satan (world) tempting Christ.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 (folder 90) — Jonas on Manichaeism outflanks Burroughs
mention_cards.context: Dick naming the framework that finally displaces Burroughs. Reading Hans Jonas on Manichaeism gave him a structure he judges more radical ontologically — not an invasion of the world but a doubt about whether the world is there at all. The vocabulary that follows is Jonas's: beguiling, entrapment, ensnaring, engulfing on one side; error, ignorance, sleep, intoxication and forgetfulness on his own.
mention_cards.pith: This very slightly resembles Burroughs, but is much more radical (ontologically speaking).
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 (folder 90) — radical acosmism: living info as world
mention_cards.context: Dick's radical acosmism, arrived at after watching the I Ching do what he had seen the plasmate do in 3-74. Living information is divine, and so is he — and it still controls us, on Burroughs's authority, while wearing the world as a disguise. The passage ends with the reversal of appearances that governs the late work: the enslaver appears beautiful, Christ appears as trash and pain.
mention_cards.pith: This living info is divine but so am I. + it controls us (as Burroughs teaches); more, it assumes the guise of [being a] world
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Exegesis, April 16, 1981 (folder 53) — the cut-up method and Hagia Sophia reading Torah
mention_cards.context: The cut-up method given a theological cause. Dick is working out how Hagia Sophia and the Torah function together in creation: if she reads the book aloud, that reading is the world. It follows that any fragment of text is already inside the narration — which is why, he reasons, Burroughs's randomised texts produce narrative rather than noise. He connects it to a dream of galley pages bearing a message about a writer in Marin County.
mention_cards.pith: This is why -as William Burroughs found- when any written text is cut up + rejoined at random, a narrative results.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Bill Sarill, January 12, 1976 — Selected Letters 1975–1976
mention_cards.context: The earliest Burroughs reference in the archive, and it is about business, not ideas — eight months before Dick reads him. Doubleday planned to Xerox the manuscript of A Scanner Darkly and send it to literary figures with standing among college readers, and left Dick to make the approaches. His difficulty, stated plainly to a friend, is that he knows no one outside science fiction, and that Doubleday does not want the novel read by anyone inside it.
mention_cards.pith: They want people like William Burroughs, Kurt Vonnegut—all the counterculture cult heroes to read it.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: Earliest dated Burroughs reference found in the archive. Note that it is about publishing, not ideas: eight months before Dick reads him.

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Sharon Jarvis, January 12, 1976 — Selected Letters 1975–1976
mention_cards.context: The same problem, put to his agent on the same day. Lacking access to the writers Doubleday wants, Dick falls back on review quotations, and copies out one from Oui that pairs him with Burroughs. The comparison is the magazine's, not his — worth noting, since it is the earliest instance of the pairing in the archive and it circulated for years, reappearing in the fanzine PKD Otaku.
mention_cards.pith: In many ways, Phil Dick is to psychedelics and science fiction what William Burroughs is to hard drugs and mainstream literature.
mention_cards.speaker: Oui, quoted by PKD
mention_cards.editorial_note: Dick quoting a review in Oui. The comparison is the magazine’s, not his.

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Kate Wenner, Rolling Stone College Papers, October 5, 1979 — Selected Letters 1977–1979
mention_cards.context: Dick thanking the editor of Rolling Stone College Papers for the first issue, which carried his story "Strange Memories of Death" alongside an article on Burroughs and an interview with him. The remark is the only place in the archive where Dick claims the Beat affiliation for himself, and he does it in passing, as a reason the two pieces sit well together.
mention_cards.pith: his interview leads right into my story inasmuch as he discusses the rebellion during the Fifties and the Beats, of which I was one.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Ben Adams, January 20, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982
mention_cards.context: Advice to a beginning writer, and a rare direct statement of whom Dick thought worth reading. The list is short and entirely outside science fiction. The surrounding counsel is practical to the point of bluntness — write what you know, keep a journal, ignore negative criticism — which is the register in which Burroughs appears here: as a working model of prose, not as a theorist.
mention_cards.pith: read the great prose writers: Faulkner, Hemingway, Hunter S. Thompson, William Burroughs, Saul Bellow, Herbert Gold.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Richard E. Geis, February 20, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982
mention_cards.context: Written to the fanzine editor Richard E. Geis while Dick was defending VALIS against the charge of being simply autobiography. He works through the problem of the first person by way of Henry Miller, then states what he was actually attempting: an old form, the picaresque, carrying modern voices. Burroughs is named as a source of the prose, alongside Hunter S. Thompson and his own A Scanner Darkly — the only forward-running debt Dick ever claims.
mention_cards.pith: a new kind of blending of the ancient picaresque form with certain modern elements associated with Hunter S. Thompson and William S. Burroughs
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Patricia Warrick, February 23, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982
mention_cards.context: Three days later, the same account to the scholar Patricia Warrick, with the politics attached. Dick has been in conflict with Ursula K. Le Guin and with Lem, and frames his own work as protest art set against official culture — which is what the vernacular in VALIS is for. The Burroughs debt is stylistic and specific, and it sits inside a description of VALIS as a novel about madness and God told by a madman with whom Dick identifies.
mention_cards.pith: It is a picaresque novel blended with new elements derived from William Burroughs, Hunter S. Thompson
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Brig Elliot, April 15, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982
mention_cards.context: The opening of the most important document in the dossier: Dick's reply to a correspondent named Brig Elliot, written on 15 April 1981, one day before the Exegesis entry that states the reversal. He confirms what he has read and what he understands by it — and then dates his own observation of the phenomenon to 1971, before he knew of Burroughs, which is the single strongest piece of evidence against reading A Scanner Darkly as Burroughs-influenced.
mention_cards.pith: Back in 1971 before I knew of Burroughs I noted a thinking dysfunction or occlusion in people involved with drugs; I deal with this in A SCANNER DARKLY.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: Dated one day before the Exegesis entry that states the reversal. Dick also dates his own observation of occlusion to 1971, "before I knew of Burroughs".

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Brig Elliot, April 15, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982
mention_cards.context: The fairest sentence Dick ever wrote about anyone he disagreed with. He has just described a dysfunction in which the self-monitoring circuit is itself compromised — so the impairment cannot notice itself — and turns to Burroughs's explanation. He declines it and refuses to dismiss it in the same breath, then separates the two things that can be judged separately: the description of the problem, and the account of its cause.
mention_cards.pith: he states the problem correctly, although perhaps his analysis of the cause is faulty; still, merely to be aware of the problem is to achieve a great deal
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Brig Elliot, April 15, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982
mention_cards.context: Later in the same letter, and this is where the disagreement is named. Dick has found accounts of occlusion in ancient sources — the Cave of Treasures, Adam deprived of his bright nature, Calvin as quoted in the VALIS tractate — and argues that if the condition exists it is very old, which removes the need for an invasion. The difference is then reduced to a single question of valence, with a third possibility left open: that the information life form has no interest in us either way and merely rides our traffic.
mention_cards.pith: it is benign; it does not occlude us; on the contrary: it informs us
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Patricia Warrick, August 18, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982
mention_cards.context: Four months later, to Patricia Warrick, and the formulation has hardened into metaphysics. Dick corrects his own line in VALIS that the universe consists of information: what he should have said is that rolling the universe back to its ontological source yields the Word or Torah. The disagreement with Burroughs is no longer about whether the information life form is friendly but about where it stands — not an invader from outside but the level above.
mention_cards.pith: This life form has not invaded our universe (as William Burroughs supposes) but is the source of our universe, one level higher
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick

mention_cards.citation: Letter to Patricia Warrick, August 18, 1981 — Selected Letters 1980–1982
mention_cards.context: The last dated Burroughs reference in the archive, at the close of the same letter. Dick describes the meta-abstraction by which he says he rolled the physical universe back to the Uttered Word, arriving at "word" as the right translation of Logos — and then measures the distance from Burroughs in a single sentence, with an exclamation mark. Language is the origin of the world, not the parasite on it.
mention_cards.pith: This view is a far cry from Burroughs’ notion that we have been invaded by an information virus that is making us stupid!
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: The last dated Burroughs reference in the archive.

mention_cards.citation: Gregg Rickman, Philip K. Dick: In His Own Words — interview
mention_cards.context: The only interview in the archive where Dick discusses the word virus, and the tone is entirely different from the notebooks: relaxed, and slightly amused. Talking to Gregg Rickman about Chesterton's The Man Who Was Thursday, he distinguishes his own taste in conspiracy from the ordinary kind, and files Burroughs firmly under the ordinary kind. He and Robert Anton Wilson, he says, prefer benign conspiracies — and then notes that this is much harder to explain psychologically than paranoia.
mention_cards.pith: the parasitic information virus which has afflicted our minds and made us all stupid. They’ve taken over the planet. That’s cool.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: NEW in the sweep. The only interview in the archive where Dick discusses the word virus. He classes it as a malign-conspiracy belief and contrasts it with the benign conspiracy he and Robert Anton Wilson prefer — consistent with the 1981 letters, and a third venue for the same argument.

mention_cards.citation: PKD, "How to Build a Universe That Doesn’t Fall Apart Two Days Later" (1978)
mention_cards.context: From the 1978 essay, published in Dick's lifetime, in which he defines reality as that which does not go away when you stop believing in it. The surrounding argument is about manufactured pseudo-worlds delivered by media into the heads of viewers, and about how much of television is received subliminally. It is his clearest statement that language is the instrument of control — and the authority he cites is Orwell, not Burroughs. Lapoujade reads this passage as Dick's proximity to Burroughs; Dick's own attribution says otherwise, and both belong on the record.
mention_cards.pith: The basic tool for the manipulation of reality is the manipulation of words. If you can control the meaning of words, you can control the people who must use the words.
mention_cards.speaker: Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.editorial_note: Dick’s clearest statement of language-as-control, written the same year as "William Burroughs is correct" — but he credits Orwell, not Burroughs. Lapoujade reads this passage as proximity to Burroughs (register C); Dick’s own attribution is register A. Do not collapse the two.

mention_cards.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (1989)
mention_cards.context: The single most useful paragraph of biography in the dossier. Sutin describes K. W. Jeter's role after the two men resumed their friendship in late 1976: unpersuaded by Dick's religious theories but willing to complicate them. It is Jeter who supplies the Burroughs parallel — which identifies the "KW" credited throughout the September 1976 Exegesis entries — and Jeter with whom Dick actually performed a cut-up experiment, on Moby Dick, Roderick Thorp's The Detective, and the Book of Acts. That last text is the one Dick elsewhere insists generated itself in Flow My Tears.
mention_cards.pith: He called attention to the similarities between Phil’s novels and those of William Burroughs-such as an invading alien virus occluding human faculties (for Burroughs, the virus is language).
mention_cards.speaker: Lawrence Sutin
mention_cards.editorial_note: THE key biographical finding. Sutin identifies the "KW" of the 1976 Exegesis entries as K.W. Jeter, reports that Jeter drew the Burroughs parallel, and records that Dick and Jeter performed their own cut-up experiment on Moby Dick, Roderick Thorp’s The Detective and the Book of Acts — the same Acts material Dick elsewhere claims generated itself in Flow My Tears.

mention_cards.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions (1989)
mention_cards.context: Sutin placing Burroughs among Dick's reading, in a list that runs from physics papers to the Bhagavad Gita by way of Binswanger. The passage is evidence for breadth, not for chronology: no date is attached, and it sits beside Sutin's note that Dick would name Stendhal, Flaubert and Maupassant before any science fiction writer when asked about influence. It should be read against Dick's own statement that he did not know Burroughs in 1971.
mention_cards.pith: Throughout his life the range of his reading was virtually limitless, from technical papers on physics to Binswanger’s daseinanalyse to Jung, Kant, William Burroughs, the Bible, the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Bhagavad Gita.
mention_cards.speaker: Lawrence Sutin
mention_cards.editorial_note: Sutin places Burroughs in Dick’s lifelong reading. Note the tension with Dick’s own statement to Brig Elliot that he did not know Burroughs before 1971–76; Sutin gives no date for the reading.

mention_cards.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions (1989)
mention_cards.context: Sutin using Burroughs to frame Ubik — the biographer's comparison, not Dick's. The context is Runciter's graffito and the impossibility of knowing which side of the half-life boundary anyone is on, including Runciter himself. Sutin's point is that the novel declines to answer, and that Ubik itself, hard to come by and requiring something like faith, is what is offered instead of an answer.
mention_cards.pith: A student once asked William Burroughs if he believed in life after death. Burroughs asked back: How do you know you’re not dead already?
mention_cards.speaker: Lawrence Sutin
mention_cards.editorial_note: Sutin uses a Burroughs anecdote to frame Ubik’s central question. This is the biographer’s comparison, not Dick’s.

mention_cards.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions (1989)
mention_cards.context: A judgement on style, and it goes against Burroughs. Discussing the antidrug theme of A Scanner Darkly — and Dick's 1973 offer of assistance to the Department of Justice — Sutin argues that Dick captured sixties drug dialogue more accurately than Burroughs did in The Soft Machine and The Wild Boys, and illustrates it with Ernie Luckman's scheme for smuggling hashish carved into the shape of a man.
mention_cards.pith: William Burroughs employs a junkie patois that is part forties Times Square, part private eye, part laconic Beat Burroughs. Vivid and sharp, but not the way it sounded at the time.
mention_cards.speaker: Lawrence Sutin
mention_cards.editorial_note: Sutin judges Dick’s drug dialogue more accurate than Burroughs’.

mention_cards.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions (1989)
mention_cards.context: Sutin on the cost of genre classification, with Burroughs as the control case. The argument is that the same books would have been received as literature under different names, and it is followed by a Borges example running the other way — "Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius" would have been shelved as science fiction had Dick written it.
mention_cards.pith: They were marketed as SF, but if, say, William Burroughs and Thomas Pynchon, respectively, had written them, they would have been mainstream.
mention_cards.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

mention_cards.citation: David Lapoujade, Worlds Built to Fall Apart: Versions of Philip K. Dick
mention_cards.context: The core of the only sustained scholarly treatment in the archive. Lapoujade has been arguing that for Dick the left hemisphere is dedicated to the programming of the psyche, the brain becoming a servo-mechanism shaped by linguistic and numeric algorithms. He quotes Dick's "How to Build a Universe" passage and sets Burroughs beside it, with the line from Nova Express — word begets image, and image is virus.
mention_cards.pith: On this point, Dick is rather close to William S. Burroughs, for whom the words of a language are tools used for taking control of brains and taking over their ability to construct realities.
mention_cards.speaker: David Lapoujade
mention_cards.editorial_note: The most sustained scholarly treatment of the connection in this archive. Lapoujade quotes Burroughs’ "Word begets image and image is virus" (Nova Express) beside Dick’s "How to Build a Universe" passage.

mention_cards.citation: David Lapoujade, Worlds Built to Fall Apart
mention_cards.context: Lapoujade's causal claim, and the most contestable thing on this page. Having established the resemblance, he explains it as convergence rather than influence: both men read Korzybski, whose general semantics describes how language imposes bivalent Aristotelian logic on analogical experience. The archive holds no direct evidence of Dick reading Korzybski, and the passage Lapoujade quotes credits Orwell — so this belongs in the register of scholarly argument, not established fact.
mention_cards.pith: This proximity between Dick and Burroughs stems in part from their readings of Alfred Korzybski
mention_cards.speaker: David Lapoujade
mention_cards.editorial_note: Lapoujade’s causal claim: Korzybski is a shared source rather than Burroughs being a source for Dick. The archive contains no direct evidence either way for Dick’s Korzybski reading; treat as register C.

mention_cards.citation: David Lapoujade, Worlds Built to Fall Apart
mention_cards.context: Lapoujade on proliferating artifacts — simulacra, androids, the synthetic animals of Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, Molinari's spare bodies in Now Wait for Last Year — and the moment where copies stop being copies and become the world. The Burroughs comparison is doing specific work: it supplies the mechanism by which junk spreads, and the sickness it carries with it.
mention_cards.pith: As in Burroughs, the “trash” has the propagative power of a virus
mention_cards.speaker: David Lapoujade

mention_cards.citation: David Lapoujade, Worlds Built to Fall Apart
concepts: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch
mention_cards.context: Lapoujade on drugs as an instrument of control rather than of escape, following from his argument that whoever controls the transmission of information controls what gets called reality. He reads The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch as the clearest case: two drugs sold by two dealers described as rival divinities, one of them offering a communion that delivers its users into a standardised world.
mention_cards.pith: There are no soft drugs in Dick. There are only hard drugs that attack the brain directly and take control of it, as in Burroughs.
mention_cards.speaker: David Lapoujade

mention_cards.citation: David Lapoujade, Worlds Built to Fall Apart
mention_cards.context: A structural parallel drawn from Naked Lunch rather than from the Nova trilogy. Lapoujade distinguishes the analogical, which circulates between worlds, from the digital, which is sealed inside its own codes, and finds Dick arriving independently at Burroughs's opposition between cooperatives, which create, and bureaucracies, which can only graft themselves onto what already exists, in the manner of a tapeworm.
mention_cards.pith: Dick rediscovers the distinction between cooperatives and bureaucracies that Burroughs established in _Naked Lunch_
mention_cards.speaker: David Lapoujade

mention_cards.citation: Andrew M. Butler, Philip K. Dick (Pocket Essentials, rev. ed.)
mention_cards.context: Butler reading the Author's Note of A Scanner Darkly, in which Dick describes drug users as children punished for playing, and includes himself among them. The comparison is to the prefatory testimony Burroughs attached to Naked Lunch — the addict's account of his own sickness, offered as a warning. Butler's point is that Dick's novel is neither an anti-drug tract nor an advertisement, and the Burroughs parallel is what lets him say so.
mention_cards.pith: Compare this to William S Burroughs’ testimony about his own sickness and the word to the wise which forms a health warning to _Naked Lunch._
mention_cards.speaker: Andrew M. Butler
mention_cards.editorial_note: Butler compares the Author’s Note of A Scanner Darkly to Burroughs’ prefatory testimony in Junky.

mention_cards.citation: Erik Davis in Details, quoted as a jacket endorsement on Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
mention_cards.context: Reception rather than argument, and included because it shows what the pairing came to mean after Dick's death. Erik Davis's line, written for Details, was picked up as a jacket endorsement and reprinted for years — here on an edition of Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, and again in the fanzine Simulacrum Meltdown. Burroughs functions in it as the writer against whom Dick's stature is measured: a succession, not an influence.
mention_cards.pith: If the ’70s and ’80s…belonged to William Burroughs, the millennium belongs to Philip K. Dick.
mention_cards.speaker: Erik Davis
mention_cards.editorial_note: Reception rather than argument: Burroughs as the writer Dick is measured against. The same line is reprinted in the fanzine Simulacrum Meltdown 3, there in the present tense ("belong to William Burroughs").

passages.passage_text: … But they resumed their friendship in late 1976, after a three-year hiatus, and now Jeter played the gadfly role to perfection. A former antiwar activist in the Socialist Workers Party, Jeter was little drawn to the religious theories Phil fashioned from his 2-3-74 experiences. But Jeter knew how to stoke the theoretical fires, adding complexities on top of Phil’s own. He called attention to the similarities between Phil’s novels and those of William Burroughs-such as an invading alien virus occluding human faculties (for Burroughs, the virus is language). contradictions.summary: In 1976 Dick reports throwing off a word virus that had infected him; in 1981 he denies that any information virus occludes anyone.
contradictions.explanation: The headline reversal, and the least complicated of the four. The 1976 entry treats 3-74 as remission from an infection Burroughs correctly diagnosed. The 1981 entry keeps both components — living information, and occlusion — but severs the causal link and reassigns living information to the side of the remedy. Neither reading is ever retracted.

contradictions.summary: The April 1981 sitting that states the reversal also keeps the occluding virus, in the same pages.
contradictions.explanation: Within the same sitting Dick writes that Torah is "like an occluding information virus", that the living information "controls us (as Burroughs teaches)", and that Satan "ensnared him as the info virus of Burroughs". He does not choose between the readings; he sets a living hyper-information against the occluding one and leaves them in combat. Any summary presenting April 1981 as a settled reversal is tidier than the notebooks.

contradictions.summary: In October 1978 the virus is the disease and the cure, in the same section.
contradictions.explanation: One passage calls the information virus "antitoxic, de-occlusive" and maps it onto four of Dick's own novels as the thing that lifts the occlusion. Another, in the same section, says "Burroughs is right" and that the occluding life form "enslaves us and kills us". A third rejects the frame outright: "This is no information virus; this is blindness." The 1978 material is not a stage between 1976 and 1981; it already contains both poles.

contradictions.summary: To a correspondent Dick refuses to call Burroughs's theory paranoia; to himself he had already named paranoia as one of its two sources.
contradictions.explanation: The 1978 Exegesis entry attributes his own "contamination" reading to Burroughs's theory plus "paranoia and paranoiac fear". The 1981 letter to Brig Elliot declines to dismiss the same theory "as mere paranoia on his part". Strictly the two are compatible — one is about Dick, the other about Burroughs — but they show the difference between what the notebooks say and what the letters concede.
